passage: A familiar story about civic life holds that ordinary people have withdrawn from it. Where their grandparents joined lodges, unions, parents' associations and choral societies, attended meetings and stood for office in them, people today are said to stay at home, absorbed in private amusements and too busy or too distrustful to join anything. The story is usually told as a matter of individual choice and individual failing, and the remedies proposed follow naturally from it: people should be encouraged, shamed or gently nudged back into joining.

There is another way to read much of the same evidence. What has declined is not association as such but a particular form of it: the federation of local branches, each with its own officers, meetings and dues, linked through elected delegates to regional and national bodies. In its place, many of the organisations that now claim to speak for citizens are run by professional staff from a central office. They recruit supporters through mailing lists and advertisements, ask them for money rather than time, and consult them, if at all, through surveys. Their membership lists may be long, but a member is someone who has made a payment, not someone who has attended a meeting, and nothing in the organisation's routine requires that members ever meet one another.

Read this way, the decline is less a withdrawal from below than a transformation from above. Organisations discovered that it was cheaper and more effective, at least for the purposes of lobbying and publicity, to raise money from many distant supporters than to sustain an expensive structure of local branches with their own halls, officers and opinions. Funders, too, preferred bodies with a clear national voice and a small, accountable staff, and the habits of professional management spread from one organisation to the next. The people who drifted away from the older associations may not have rejected participation at all; they may simply have been offered fewer occasions for it.

The distinction matters because the federated association did something its successors do not. It taught people with no political ambitions how to run a meeting, keep minutes, manage a budget, argue for a motion and accept defeat when it was voted down. These were not trivial accomplishments; they were the ordinary apprenticeship of democratic citizenship for many who would never hold public office. It also tied the local to the national: a member in a small town could, through a chain of elected representatives, influence what the national body did. A donor to a professionally managed organisation may support its aims with real conviction, but she learns none of these skills and holds no comparable thread of influence over what is done in her name.

It would be easy to turn this into nostalgia, and nostalgia would mislead. Many of the old associations excluded women or people of the wrong background, and their local meetings could be stifling and petty. The new organisations, for their part, have often been more effective at changing laws. Nor have people stopped gathering; they form online groups and informal networks with remarkable ease. But these are seldom built to govern themselves through elected officers and binding votes. If the loss is real, it is the loss of a school of self-government, and it will not be repaired by urging individuals to join more. It would require organisations to find reasons, and funders to give them reasons, to want members who turn up.

passage: It is often said that the orderly queue reveals something about a people's character, as if patience were a national trait passed down with the language. The explanation is flattering to those who queue well and insulting to those who do not, and it is mostly wrong. A queue is better understood as a small institution: a shared rule, first come first served, enforced by no official and sustained by people who mostly do not know one another and will never meet again. What needs explaining, therefore, is not why some nations are supposedly virtuous but why such a rule, lacking any formal sanction, holds at all among strangers.

Part of the answer is that the queue makes its own rule visible. Everyone can see the line, everyone can see their place in it, and anyone who pushes in is caught in the act before an audience that has every reason to object. The penalty is rarely more than a sharp word or a collective stare, yet it is usually enough, because the offender cannot pretend not to know the rule. Compare a crowd waiting at the doors of a bus, where no line has formed. Here the same people who would wait patiently at a ticket counter will often jostle, not because they have become selfish but because no one can say with confidence who arrived first. Without a visible order there is nothing to defend and no clear offence to resent.

This suggests that the strength of an informal norm depends less on the virtue of those who follow it than on how legible it makes compliance and violation. Managers of busy offices seem to have grasped this when they introduced numbered tickets: the ticket does not change anyone's character, but it turns an ambiguous crowd into an order that each person can check. Railings, painted footprints and single winding lines that feed many counters work in the same way. The same logic explains why a queue that winds around a corner, so that newcomers cannot tell where it ends, tends to generate precisely the disputes that a visible line prevents. Such devices are inexpensive, and they succeed by removing doubt rather than by threatening punishment.

None of this means that the queue is the fairest possible way to allocate a scarce service. It rewards those with time to spare and ignores urgency; a hospital that treated patients strictly in order of arrival would be orderly and indefensible. Nor should the absence of lines be read as disorder, since a crowd may follow subtler conventions that an outsider fails to notice. The point is narrower. Where people do accept first come first served, the rule survives among strangers because it can be seen, and it falters where it cannot.

passage: It is often said that explaining a joke kills it, and anyone who has tried to rescue a failed pun by spelling out its double meaning knows that the saying is true as far as it goes. The listener nods, perhaps smiles politely, but the laugh that should have come does not. The usual inference drawn from this experience is that humour is a fragile, almost mystical thing, which analysis can only damage, and that the serious study of comedy is a contradiction in terms. The experience is real; the inference does not follow from it.

Consider why the explanation fails. A joke typically sets up one way of understanding a situation and then, in a single move, reveals that a second way was available all along. The pleasure lies largely in the listener's own discovery of the second meaning, in the sudden reorganisation that happens in his head rather than on the page. Explanation takes this work away from him. It hands over the result without the leap, much as being told the answer to a riddle deprives one of the satisfaction of solving it. The joke is not killed because it has been examined; it is killed because the examination has been done for the listener, before he could do it himself, at the very moment that was meant to be his.

Seen in this way, the failure of explained jokes tells us something about humour, namely that it depends on an active contribution from the audience, and this is exactly the kind of thing analysis can discover. There is nothing self-defeating in studying how jokes work, any more than there is in studying how riddles work. The student of comedy who analyses a routine afterwards does not expect to laugh at the analysis; he expects to understand the laugh he has already had. The two activities are simply different, and the second does not undo the first.

There is even a case for explanation in the moment, under certain conditions. A joke that turns on an unfamiliar word, a local custom or an allusion to a book the listener has not read cannot produce its leap, because one of the two meanings is not available to him at all. Here a brief explanation does not perform the leap on the listener's behalf; it only supplies the missing ground from which he can make it, and a listener who has been told what the allusion refers to will sometimes laugh a moment later, on his own. The skilled explainer, like the skilled comedian, knows how much to say and when to stop.

options.B: the explanation offered is usually far less clever than the joke it tries to rescue.
options.C: most listeners resent being told something that they were perfectly able to work out.
options.D: the listener is denied the chance to discover the second meaning for himself.

passage: The familiar story of urbanisation runs in one direction. People leave the countryside for the city, struggle for a generation in its least desirable quarters, and are eventually absorbed, their children speaking the city's idiom and regarding the village as a place of grandparents and holidays. Migration, on this account, is a passage with a beginning and an end, and the only question worth asking about a migrant is how far along it he has come. The story is not false; it describes what happened to many families in many countries. But it has acquired the status of a norm, against which other patterns are measured and found wanting, and this has made it difficult to see a pattern that is, in much of the world, at least as common.

A large number of those who work in cities never complete the journey the story describes. They come for a season of construction or a few years in a factory, return for the harvest, a wedding or an illness in the family, and come back again, sometimes to the same city and sometimes to another. Their earnings pay school fees and debts in the village; the village holds their land, their elders and, often, their spouses and children. A household can live this way for decades, and many do. Seen through the one-way story, such people are migrants who have not yet settled, a transitional population whose double life is a symptom of incomplete integration. Seen on its own terms, the pattern looks rather different: a way of spreading risk across two places, so that a lost job in the city or a failed crop in the village need not be ruinous, because the other place remains.

The distinction matters because city governments have tended to act on the first reading. A resident whose household is registered elsewhere, whose stay is irregular, and whose address is a worksite or a shared rented room is easily treated as a visitor: excluded from subsidised housing, from schools for the children who come along, from the electoral roll, and from the attention of politicians who answer to those who are on it. The exclusion then produces the very evidence that justifies it. Denied a secure foothold in the city, the circular migrant has every reason to keep the village in reserve, and the persistence of his village ties is then cited as proof that he never really belonged.

It would be a mistake to romanticise circulation in its turn. Some who move back and forth would settle in the city if they could, and return to the village only because the city offers them nothing to stay for; for them, circularity is less a strategy than a sentence. Others genuinely prefer a life lived in two places and would keep it even if the city were more welcoming. The difficulty is that from the outside the two groups look identical, and a policy designed for one will misjudge the other.

What follows is not a single programme but a change in the condition attached to belonging. A city that made its entitlements portable, that allowed a worker to enrol his children in school without proving permanent residence, and that encouraged cheap rental housing suited to stays of months rather than decades would serve both groups at once. It would allow those who wish to settle to do so, and those who wish to circulate to circulate without penalty. What it would cease to do is demand that a person surrender one home as the price of being recognised in another.

options.C: a choice made chiefly because wages in the city are so much higher than anything the village can offer.

passage: Imagine a small-town bank that is entirely sound: its loans are prudent and its borrowers will repay, although those loans run for years while its deposits can be withdrawn on any day. Suppose a rumour spreads that this institution is in trouble. Each depositor now faces a simple calculation: if others withdraw and I do not, my bank may have to sell its loans in a hurry and at a loss, leaving me with little, whereas if I withdraw first, I lose nothing. It is therefore rational to run whether or not the rumour is true, and once enough people run, the rumour becomes true. Such a bank fails not because it was unsound but because it was believed to be.

Deposit insurance is the classic answer, because a guarantee from the state, up to some limit, alters the calculation entirely. A depositor who stays put loses nothing even if her bank collapses, so she has no reason to join a run, and because no one runs, the guarantee is seldom called upon. Seen in this light, insurance looks almost like a free lunch: a promise that, by being believed, makes its own fulfilment unnecessary.

The objection is familiar. Insured depositors have no reason to ask what their bank does with their money, and a bank whose depositors do not ask can take risks that it would otherwise have to justify to them. The guarantee that ends panics may thus encourage the very recklessness that makes failures likely. Critics conclude that deposit insurance trades a visible problem for a hidden one, and some would scale it back so that depositors once again have a reason to pay attention.

The objection is sound as far as it goes, but it rests on a curious picture of who disciplined banks before guarantees existed. Ordinary depositors were never skilled readers of loan books; what they were skilled at was panic. The discipline they supplied was indiscriminate, falling on sound and unsound banks alike once fear took hold, as the town bank illustrates. If insured depositors stop watching, little genuine scrutiny is lost, and the task passes to those equipped for it: supervisors with the power to inspect, and the large uninsured creditors whose money remains at stake. The lesson of the objection is not that guarantees are a mistake but that they must be paired with oversight, and that the limit on cover matters a great deal, since it decides who still has a reason to care.

passage: A long tradition in philosophy, going back at least to Locke, holds that what makes me the same person as some earlier individual is neither the persistence of my body nor that of some hidden soul but memory. I am the person who sat that examination twenty years ago because I can remember sitting it, from the inside, as something I did. The view has an attractive modesty. It ties personal identity to something we actually experience rather than to an unobservable substance, and it appears to match our intuitions about imaginary cases: if all of my memories were somehow transferred into another body, many people feel that it is I who would wake up in it.

The theory faces two well-known difficulties. The first concerns chains of memory. Imagine a woman of eighty who vividly remembers her first day as a teacher at thirty, and suppose that the teacher of thirty could still recall a childhood accident at six of which the woman of eighty remembers nothing. On a strict memory criterion the old woman is the teacher and the teacher is the child, yet the old woman is not the child, since she remembers nothing of her. Identity cannot behave this way: if A is the same as B and B is the same as C, then A is the same as C. The second difficulty is subtler. To distinguish a genuine memory of sitting an examination from a vivid but false impression of having sat it, we seem to need to know already that the rememberer is the person who sat it. Memory, apparently, presupposes the identity it was supposed to explain.

The first objection can be met by allowing overlapping chains of memory, rather than direct memory, to carry identity; the second is much harder to escape. Yet it is worth asking what the defenders of the memory view were really after. Their deepest conviction was not a thesis about the logic of identity but a claim about what makes the past matter to a person. A past that I can recall, whose intentions I have carried out and whose anxieties still shape me, is mine in a way that a past I share only bodily is not.

Seen in this light, the theory fails as an account of identity and succeeds as an account of something else: the degree to which a person is connected to her own history. That connection comes in degrees and can weaken, which identity, being all or nothing, cannot do. The old woman is the child she once was, but she is far less connected to that child than to the teacher. Many of our practical concerns, from the keeping of old promises to the sense of responsibility for what we did long ago, may track this connection more closely than they track identity itself.

options.B: identity must hold from one end of a chain to the other, whereas direct memory need not.
options.C: memories might be transferred into another body, which would make two quite different people one and the same person.
options.D: telling a genuine memory from a convincing false one seems to require knowing already who the rememberer is.

passage: It has become a commonplace, in philosophy as much as in popular psychology, that a self is a kind of story. On this view a person is not a thing that persists beneath her experiences but the narrative she composes from them: the account of where she came from, what she has struggled against and where she is heading. The claim is usually advanced in two forms at once. The descriptive form says that human beings do in fact understand themselves through stories. The normative form adds that they ought to, and that a life which cannot be gathered into a coherent narrative is in some way impoverished or broken.

The descriptive claim is plausible for many people, but its generality is doubtful. Some people report that they do not experience their lives as a plot at all. They feel little connection with the person they were a decade ago, find the invitation to tell their life story faintly baffling, and live with their attention fixed on present tasks and relationships. Nor is there any obvious sense in which their lives go worse: they form attachments, deliberate carefully and take responsibility for their conduct, only without experiencing their existence as an unfolding plot. It would be rash to assume that such people are simply unreflective, or that they are concealing a narrative they would rather not acknowledge. Their testimony is at least as credible as that of people who say the opposite, and it suggests that narrative self-understanding is one way of being a self rather than the condition of being one.

The normative claim is more troubling. Stories have shapes, and the pressure to give one's life a shape is a pressure to select. Episodes that fit the arc are remembered and retold; those that do not are discarded or reinterpreted. Autobiographical memory is already reconstructive, and a governing narrative supplies it with a principle of selection that is rarely examined. A person who has told herself for years that she is someone who overcomes adversity will find it difficult to see the occasions on which she gave up, and harder still to learn from them. The demand for coherence can thus become a demand for a flattering kind of forgetting. A novelist may legitimately omit whatever does not serve the plot; a life conducted on the same principle may lose precisely the evidence it most needs.

None of this means that narrative has no place. Making a promise requires regarding one's future self as continuous with one's present intention, and recovering from bereavement or injury often involves finding a way to tell what happened so that it can be lived with. Understanding other people, too, frequently depends on grasping the story they take themselves to be in. These are genuine goods, and a person who could never assemble any part of her past into an account would be at a real disadvantage.

But the goods enumerated here are those of an instrument, not of an essence. We use stories to bind ourselves, to heal and to understand, and we can use them well or badly, often or seldom. To say that the self simply is its story makes the instrument indispensable, and it turns a difference in temperament into a deficiency. The more modest view leaves room both for lives that are lived largely in the present and for the episodes that refuse to fit, and it may well be the more truthful of the two.

options.A: a person is a thing that persists unchanged beneath the experiences she has over a lifetime.
options.B: stories should be used only for making promises, recovering from loss and understanding others.
options.C: a life that cannot be gathered into a coherent story is in some way deficient.
options.D: human beings do in fact come to understand themselves through stories about their lives.

passage: It is widely believed that there is a window for learning languages, open in early childhood and closed by adolescence, after which a new language can be studied but never truly acquired. The belief has some foundation. On average, people who begin a second language in early childhood end up closer to native-like command than people who begin as adults, and the difference is clearest in pronunciation: a late learner who has spoken a language fluently for decades will often still carry an accent that a child immigrant lost within a few years. What the evidence supports, however, is a slope rather than a window. The image of a door that slams shut at a fixed age is the part of the popular picture least able to survive scrutiny.

Several things complicate the story that age alone is at work. Children and adults who move to a new country do not learn under the same conditions. The child is enrolled in school, surrounded for hours each day by speakers of the new language and given every incentive to sound like them; the adult often works among speakers of her first language, uses the new one for limited purposes and has an identity already settled in the old. When late learners are compared with early ones, these differences in the quantity and character of exposure travel along with age, and it is hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains. Where adults are immersed in the way children are, some reach levels that the stricter versions of the window theory say should be out of reach.

It also matters what is being measured. Accent appears most sensitive to the age of first exposure, and some aspects of grammar, such as fine judgements about word endings, seem sensitive too. Vocabulary, by contrast, goes on growing throughout life in a first language and a second alike, and adults often learn the early stages of a new language faster than young children do, because they bring better memory strategies and a developed grasp of how languages work. A single critical period for language as a whole therefore looks less plausible than a set of different sensitivities, declining at different rates for different components.

None of this makes early exposure unimportant, and a parent who can give a child two languages from the start gives something valuable. But the window image has costs of its own. It persuades adults that serious learning is no longer open to them, so that they invest less and expect little, and then treats the resulting modest achievement as confirmation. A more accurate picture, in which age makes some things harder and a few things much harder without closing the door at any fixed point, is less dramatic but more useful.

options.C: explaining why adults learn the early stages of a new language faster than young children usually manage to do.
options.D: arguing that adult immigrants fall short in a new language chiefly because they are not immersed in it as children are.

passage: Few ideas feel more natural than the distinction between home and work. We leave one for the other in the morning and return in the evening, and much of our moral vocabulary depends on the contrast: home is where we are valued for who we are, work where we are valued for what we produce. Yet for most of recorded history, in most agrarian and artisan societies, the distinction would have puzzled the people who lived in households. The house was where the work was done.

Consider a weaver's dwelling in a pre-industrial town, or a farmstead in the countryside. The looms or the dairy stood beside the hearth, and the people who ate at the table included not only parents and children but apprentices, servants and labourers who lived under the same roof and the same authority. The head of the household was at once father, employer and, in a limited sense, magistrate, answerable to the wider community for the conduct of everyone in his charge. Records of such households often used the word family to mean this whole working unit, and a reader who assumes that it meant blood relatives alone will misread them badly. Children worked as soon as they were able, carding wool or minding animals, and learning a trade was part of growing up in the house rather than something that began when a child left it.

None of this should be romanticised. The working household was a hierarchy, often a harsh one, in which servants could be beaten and wives had little legal standing apart from their husbands. Nor was it universal: the poorest labourers, who owned no tools and rented a single room, had little to bring home but their wages. The point is not that the old arrangement was better, but that it was different in kind, and that the difference matters for how we read later history.

When production moved into workshops, mills and offices, the household did not simply lose its economic role; it acquired a new meaning. Freed of the loom and the dairy, it could be imagined as a private refuge, governed by affection rather than discipline, and this ideal was then projected backwards as if it had always existed. The ideal was real enough for those who could afford it, but it was an ideal, not a description of the past. Laments about the decline of the family often rest on that projection. What changed over these centuries was less the strength of family feeling than the range of tasks the household was expected to perform, and a history that confuses the two will find decline where there was mainly transformation.

passage: Egalitarians hold that there is something wrong with inequality as such: that when some people are much worse off than others through no fault of their own, the situation is bad, and bad in part simply because of the gap. The most famous objection to this view asks us to consider what follows from it. Suppose that the only way to remove an inequality were to make the better off worse off, with no benefit to anyone, as if a town in which some households had gardens and others had none could reach equality only by paving over every garden. If inequality is bad in itself, then such a change would remove something bad, and so would be in one respect an improvement. Yet the change helps no one and harms many. To call it an improvement in any respect, the objectors say, is absurd.

Many philosophers have been moved by this objection to give up equality as a fundamental value. Some have adopted the view that benefits matter more the worse off their recipient is, so that a gain to a poor person counts for more than the same gain to a rich one; others hold that what matters is that everyone should have enough, after which differences cease to be of moral concern. Neither view is troubled by levelling down, since on neither does reducing the well-being of the better off, by itself, improve anything. Both also capture much of what drew people to equality in the first place, which was a concern for those who are badly off.

Yet the objection is less decisive than it is usually taken to be. The egalitarian need not claim that a levelled-down world is better all things considered, only that it is better in one respect while much worse in others. Plural values often pull apart in this way. We can think that a promise kept at terrible cost was in one respect admirable without thinking that it should have been kept. Seen this way, the levelling-down case shows only that equality is not the only thing that matters, which almost no egalitarian ever believed.

This defence succeeds, but at a price. It keeps equality as a value only by making it a strangely impersonal one: something that can make a state of affairs better while making it better for no one at all. Many will find such a value hard to care about. There is, however, another way to understand what egalitarians were after. On a relational view, the core of equality lies not in how goods are distributed but in how people stand to one another: in the absence of rank, servility and contempt, in a society where no one must bow and no one may command another merely by virtue of birth or wealth. Inequalities of resources matter on this view chiefly because, beyond some point, they turn into inequalities of standing, as when wealth buys influence over others or poverty forces deference to them.

The relational view is untouched by the levelling-down objection, because paving over gardens neither creates nor abolishes any relation of rank between neighbours. Whether it can say enough about distribution is a further question. A society might abolish titles and deference while leaving vast differences in income intact, and the relational egalitarian owes us an account of when such differences begin to corrode equal standing. But the view has at least located the value of equality in a relation between persons, which is where most of its defenders always felt it to be.

passage: Ask a collector why she keeps buying stamps, coins or toy cars long after there is any room left to display them, and the answer is rarely about the objects themselves. More often it concerns a gap: the one issue missing from a run, the single variant that would finish a set. Collecting, on this view, is less a love of things than a love of completion. The individual stamp matters because of the place it occupies in a series, and its value to the collector rises sharply as the series nears its end, often far beyond anything a buyer outside the hobby would think of paying.

Manufacturers learned long ago to exploit this. A cereal box that contains one of twelve plastic figures, a sticker album with a few deliberately scarce pages, a line of trading cards issued in waves: each turns an ordinary purchase into a step towards a whole that the buyer did not know he wanted until he was shown its outline. The empty album is the real product. Once its spaces are printed, every blank becomes a small reproach, and the purchase that fills it brings a satisfaction out of all proportion to what was bought.

It would be easy to conclude that collecting is simply a manufactured compulsion, a weakness that the market has learned to farm. That conclusion goes too far. Many of the most devoted collectors pursue series that no company ever designed: the railway timetables of a vanished line, the matchboxes of hotels that have since closed, the scattered editions of a minor poet. Here it is the collector who defines the set, deciding what counts as belonging to it and therefore what counts as missing. Such collecting is a way of ordering the world, of drawing a boundary around a scattered field and making it intelligible. Many museums began, in part, as exactly this kind of private project.

The difference between the two kinds of collecting is not the passion involved, which can be equally intense, but who holds the map. When the series is invented by a seller, completion is a target set by someone else, and the finish line is often moved just as it comes into view, with a new wave or a special edition. When the collector draws the map, completion is a judgement she makes for herself, and the pleasure lies as much in the defining as in the finding. The danger of the commercial version is not that it creates desire, since all collecting does that, but that it quietly takes the act of definition away from the person doing the collecting.

passage: Early researchers in artificial intelligence expected to begin with the easy problems and work up to the hard ones. They took easy to mean what people find easy and hard to mean what people find hard, and so they assumed that a machine which could play respectable chess or prove theorems in logic would soon be able to fold laundry or cross a cluttered room. Matters turned out almost the other way round. Programs that could beat strong players at board games arrived long before machines that could reliably pick up an unfamiliar object without crushing or dropping it. The observation that the faculties we think of as higher are the cheap ones to mechanise, while those we take for granted are expensive, has come to be described by roboticists as a paradox.

It is a paradox only if our sense of difficulty is a good guide to the difficulty of a task, and a plausible explanation is that it is not. Perception and movement have been refined over an immense evolutionary history, and they run beneath awareness, so they feel like nothing at all. Explicit reasoning is recent and effortful, and its effortfulness is precisely what we notice. The feeling of difficulty, on this account, measures how new a skill is to our species rather than how much computation it requires.

The implication for work is uncomfortable for a familiar way of ranking jobs. We tend to treat the skills of the hospital cleaner, the gardener and the care worker as basic and those of the clerk who reconciles accounts as advanced. Yet the cleaner moves through rooms that are never arranged twice in the same way and handles objects of every shape and texture, while the reconciliation follows rules that can be written down. A machine finds the second job far easier to take over than the first. Forecasts that expect automation to climb steadily upward from the bottom of the wage scale may therefore have the direction partly backwards.

Two cautions are in order. First, the paradox describes a stage of technology, not a law of nature; methods that learn from vast numbers of examples have already eroded some of the advantage that perception once enjoyed, and it would be rash to assume the boundary will stay where it is. Second, being hard to automate is not the same as being well rewarded. The skills that resist machines are often widely shared among people, and abundance keeps wages low whatever a robot can or cannot do. The paradox tells us which tasks machines will struggle with; it does not tell us that the people who perform them will prosper.

passage: It has become a commonplace that every age describes the brain in the image of its most impressive machine. When ornamental gardens were fitted with water-driven statues that moved as visitors stepped on hidden plates, nerves were pictured as pipes and the animal spirits as fluid pressed through them. When the telegraph and then the telephone exchange spread across cities, the nervous system became a network of wires, with the brain as the central office where calls were connected. In our own time it is a computer, processing information, storing memories and running programs. The pattern is real, and critics have drawn a sharp lesson from it: the metaphors are fashions, each as quaint as the last will soon appear, and the computer image will go the way of the fountain.

The lesson is half right. It is true that none of these images was the whole truth, and that each looks dated once the technology behind it is familiar. But to call them mere fashions is to miss what each one got right. The hydraulic picture captured the idea that something must travel from the senses to the centre and back to the muscles. The switchboard captured the importance of connections, of which signal is routed to which destination. The computer captured the idea that what matters about these signals is the information they carry and the transformations performed on it, rather than the stuff that carries them. Each metaphor, in other words, was adopted because it made some feature of the nervous system thinkable, and each left behind a contribution that survived its own retirement.

The real danger lies elsewhere, because a metaphor brings with it not only the features that fit but a whole set of features that come along unexamined. The computer image invites us to think of memory as storage, a place where a record sits unchanged until retrieved, when remembering appears to be closer to reconstruction, the record altered a little each time it is used. It invites a sharp division between hardware and software, when in the brain the program and the machine are hard to tell apart, since use reshapes the very structures that do the work. These are not reasons to abandon the metaphor but reasons to keep asking which of its features we are actually entitled to.

The sensible course, then, is neither to treat the current metaphor as a literal description nor to dismiss it as a passing fashion, but to use it while keeping an account of where it fails. Metaphors are tools for thinking about something that cannot be seen directly, and the history of brain science suggests that thinking without any of them is not an available option. What can be avoided is the habit of mistaking the tool for the thing.

options.D: partial agreement, accepting that no metaphor was the whole truth while denying that they were merely fashionable.

passage: The most familiar complaint about recommendation algorithms is that they trap each of us in a private enclosure. Because a system learns what a user has clicked, watched or bought, the argument runs, it will keep offering more of the same, until every listener hears only the music that confirms their existing taste and every reader meets only the opinions they already hold. On this picture the danger is fragmentation: a public that once shared a common stock of songs, books and news splinters into millions of sealed niches, each tuned to one person.

The complaint is not baseless, but it may have the main tendency of these systems the wrong way round. Most recommendation engines do not learn from one user in isolation; they learn from the aggregate behaviour of very large numbers of users, and they rank items partly by how much engagement those items have already attracted. That design creates a feedback loop. An item that gets a slight early lead is shown to more people, which earns it more engagement, which earns it still more prominence. Imagine two songs of equal appeal released on the same day, one of which happens to be picked up by a few enthusiastic listeners in its first hours. Under such a loop the small, accidental difference can harden into an enormous gap, and the second song may effectively disappear, not because anyone judged it worse but because no one was shown it.

If this is right, the characteristic risk is less fragmentation than concentration: attention pooling ever more heavily on a few items, while the vast catalogue that digital distribution made available sits largely unvisited. The early hope that online platforms would let obscure work find its small audiences depended on people actually encountering that work, and a ranking system that rewards prior popularity makes such encounters rarer than the size of the catalogue suggests.

It would be wrong to present this as something algorithms invented. Bestseller lists, radio playlists and the front tables of bookshops have always amplified what was already selling, and cultural markets have long been marked by a few large successes and many neglected works. What is new is the speed of the loop and its invisibility. A bookseller choosing what to display is a person whose choices can be questioned; a ranking produced by continuous automated feedback appears simply to report what people want, when it is partly manufacturing it. The remedy, if there is one, lies less in protecting users from their own tastes than in asking how much of what looks like popular demand is an echo of earlier exposure.

options.B: show how an accidental early advantage can grow into a large gap when ranking rewards prior engagement.
options.C: prove that listeners cannot tell apart songs of equal appeal without guidance from an algorithm.
options.D: illustrate the fragmentation of a shared public into sealed niches tuned to individual listeners.

passage: We tend to read the history of life as a long tournament in which the better designed win. On this view a lineage that disappeared must have had some flaw, and the dinosaurs, the textbook losers, are pictured as sluggish and outmoded long before their end. The picture is comfortable because it makes the present inhabitants of the earth look like deserving champions. For the most dramatic episodes in the record it is also misleading. During ordinary stretches of geological time, extinction does seem to track the qualities that adaptation produces: species with narrow diets, small ranges or slow breeding are more likely to vanish when conditions shift, and their places are taken by competitors that cope better. The great mass extinctions, in which a large fraction of species disappeared within a geologically brief interval, seem to follow different rules.

Consider the end of the Cretaceous period, when an asteroid struck the earth and the non-avian dinosaurs vanished along with many other groups. What determined survival in the aftermath was not, as far as can be told, excellence at the ways of life that had served well for millions of years. It was the possession of traits that happened to matter in a sudden catastrophe: small body size, a varied diet, the ability to shelter or to wait out a period of darkness and scarcity in a dormant state. Such traits had not been selected for their value in a catastrophe of this kind, which no living lineage had experienced. They were, from the point of view of the crisis, accidents.

The consequence is that mass extinctions can redirect the history of life in ways that ordinary selection would not. A group that had been flourishing, and that would probably have continued to flourish under normal conditions, can be swept away, while a group that had been marginal for tens of millions of years inherits an emptied world. The mammals, which had lived in the shadow of the dinosaurs for a very long time, are the familiar example. Their later success says little about whether they were superior to the non-avian dinosaurs in any absolute sense; it says that they passed through a narrow gate that the dinosaurs, for reasons unrelated to their earlier success, did not.

This does not mean that mass extinctions are pure lotteries. Survival in them is selective; it simply selects for different things. Nor does it mean that adaptation is unimportant, since the survivors went on to diversify through ordinary selection once the crisis had passed. What it does mean is that the long-run shape of life's history cannot be read as a straightforward measure of design quality. To understand why some groups are here and others are not, we need to know not only how well they fitted their world but also which rare disasters that world happened to contain.

passage: If biases are errors, it seems natural to suppose that teaching people about them should reduce them. Hence the many workshops in which managers, doctors and analysts are taken through a catalogue of the mind's failings, from anchoring to the sunk-cost fallacy, in the hope that knowing the names will help them avoid the traps. The hope is reasonable, and it is mostly disappointed. Participants usually leave such sessions able to define the biases and to spot them in descriptions of other people's reasoning. What they far less often do is reason differently when a fresh problem, dressed in unfamiliar clothes, arrives in their own work.

Part of the difficulty is that biases rarely announce themselves. A textbook problem about sunk costs is labelled, at least implicitly, by the chapter in which it appears; a real decision about whether to keep funding a struggling project comes with no such label, and with colleagues, budgets and reputations attached. Recognising a pattern in a tidy example is a different skill from noticing it in a messy situation, and teaching the first does not automatically produce the second. There is also a subtler obstacle. People readily accept that biases exist and readily see them at work in others, while judging their own conclusions to be the products of careful thought. Instruction can even sharpen this asymmetry, supplying a vocabulary for diagnosing colleagues without unsettling one's own sense of seeing clearly.

None of this shows that debiasing is hopeless. A few interventions built around repeated practice, varied examples and immediate feedback on one's own errors have produced improvements that outlasted the session, though how far they reach beyond the kinds of problem used in training remains uncertain. And there is a quieter strategy that sidesteps the question of individual reform altogether: changing the procedures within which decisions are made. A committee that collects independent estimates before discussion, or a review that requires someone to argue the case against a favoured plan, does not need its members to have become wiser. It builds the correction into the routine.

The contrast is instructive. Approaches that rely on informing the individual treat bias as a kind of ignorance, curable by knowledge. Approaches that redesign procedures treat it as a standing feature of minds working under ordinary conditions, to be managed rather than eliminated. The second view is less flattering, but it fits the evidence better, and it has the practical merit of not depending on each person's ability to catch themselves in the act.

passage: Few critical preferences are as widely shared as the preference for round characters over flat ones. A round character, in the usual formulation, has an inner life complex enough that it can change, contradict itself and still remain recognisable; a flat character is built around a single trait and can be summed up in a sentence. The first is praised as lifelike, the second tolerated as a convenience, useful for filling a drawing room or delivering a message but not to be mistaken for the real achievement of fiction.

Yet the preference rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that the novel's central business is the representation of individual inner life. That has been the business of one powerful tradition, but it is not the only thing novels do. Many of the novels readers return to are as much about a society as about a self, and a society is felt in fiction partly through the people who never change: the aunt who has said the same thing at every family dinner for thirty years, the official for whom every request is a breach of procedure. Their fixity is not a failure of imagination. It is how the novel registers the pressure of a world that does not bend, against which its few changing figures can be measured.

Flat characters also carry much of fiction's comedy, which depends on repetition. A man who responds to every misfortune by consulting the same almanac is funny the third time precisely because he could not have done otherwise. Deepen him, give him a moment of doubt about the almanac, and the joke dissolves into pathos; this may be a gain, but it is a different book. There is, too, a case that flatness is closer to ordinary experience than critics allow. Most of the people we know, we know only by a few habits and phrases, and a novel that rendered every acquaintance in the round would misrepresent how other people actually appear to us, however much it flattered our sense of their depth.

This is not to invert the hierarchy. A novel peopled entirely by flat characters would be a cartoon, and the moment when a figure we had thought simple reveals unexpected depth remains one of fiction's great effects, though it depends on our having first taken him as simple. The point is that flat and round are not grades of achievement but different tools, suited to different tasks, and a criticism that rewards only one of them will misread every novel in which both are at work.

passage: Indirect rule was presented by its architects as an act of restraint. Rather than replace the institutions of the peoples it governed, the colonial state would work through them: chiefs would keep their offices, customary courts would apply customary law, and the colonial officer would advise rather than command. The policy, most closely associated with British administration in Nigeria and later extended across much of British Africa, was cheaper than direct administration, and its defenders also claimed for it a moral advantage. It would let colonised peoples develop along their own lines instead of being turned into imitation Europeans.

The difficulty was that the institutions indirect rule claimed to preserve rarely existed in the form it required. The policy needed a chief: one identifiable person in each locality who could collect tax, supply labour and answer for order. Where centralised kingdoms existed, such a figure could be found. Where authority had been spread among councils of elders, age-grades and religious associations, as in parts of south-eastern Nigeria, officials appointed men to the role, and the so-called warrant chiefs they created had little standing in local tradition. Even where genuine rulers existed, their position changed. A king who had once had to keep the support of title-holders and rivals, and who faced the threat that subjects might desert him, now had the backing of a colonial army, and the checks that had limited him lost much of their force.

Customary law underwent a similar transformation. To be applied in courts, custom had to be written down, and the people asked to state it were usually senior men with an interest in the answer. Rules about land, marriage and inheritance that had been flexible and contested were recorded as fixed, and frequently in the form most favourable to elders against juniors and men against women. Custom that had changed with circumstances became a code that could be changed only by the administration.

It would be wrong, however, to conclude that tradition was simply invented by colonial officials and imposed on passive subjects. The elders who told officers what the custom was were pursuing their own ends, and they often succeeded; the codes bear their fingerprints as much as the administrators'. That is precisely what makes indirect rule instructive. Its most lasting effect was not the preservation of old authority, nor its outright replacement, but the creation of a new kind of authority that spoke the language of tradition while answering upward to the state rather than downward to the governed. Many post-colonial governments, finding such authority convenient, kept it.

passage: Ask someone to describe the route from their home to the nearest railway station and watch their hands. Before they have finished the first sentence, the hands will usually be tracing turns, marking distances and pointing at landmarks that are nowhere in the room. The common explanation is that gesture is a kind of visual aid for the listener, a way of adding pictures to words. On this view the hands are an accessory to communication, useful when they help an audience and idle otherwise. The explanation is not wrong, but it is incomplete, and the part it leaves out is the more interesting one.

If gesture existed only for listeners, people would stop gesturing when nobody could see them, and yet they do not: speakers on the telephone continue to move their hands, if somewhat less than they would face to face, and people who have been blind from birth gesture when they talk, even to listeners they know to be blind. A habit that persists when it can no longer inform anyone is unlikely to be explained entirely by what it does for others. The more economical conclusion is that gesture also does something for the person who produces it.

What it seems to do is lighten the work of thinking, for when people are asked to explain a problem while keeping their hands still, many speak more haltingly and struggle to find the words they want, particularly words for shapes, directions and positions. Children explaining how they solved a sum sometimes show with their hands a strategy that their words have not yet reached, pointing to two numbers together while describing a different procedure aloud. Such children are often found to be on the verge of learning the correct method, as if the hands had arrived at an idea before speech could carry it. Gesture, on this account, is not a translation of finished thought into movement; it is one of the places where thought is still being worked out.

It would be easy to overstate the case, since not every flourish of the hands is cognitive labour; some gestures are plainly social, like a wave or a shrug, and some speakers gesture little without thinking any worse for it. Nor does the evidence show that thought depends on the body in some mysterious way that rules out abstract reasoning. The claim is more modest: that for many people, much of the time, moving the hands is part of how a difficult idea gets held in mind. Even that modest claim has practical consequences, because a teacher who attends only to what a pupil says may miss what the pupil is close to understanding, and a classroom that rewards stillness may be quietly removing a tool that some children use to think.

passage: A common complaint about relative poverty lines is that they confuse poverty with inequality. If a household counts as poor whenever its income falls below, say, half of the median, then a country in which everyone became twice as rich would have exactly as many poor people as before. Critics take this as a decisive objection: a measure that cannot register a general rise in living standards, they say, is measuring the spread of incomes and calling it hardship. The objection is tidy, and it is not wrong about the arithmetic. It is wrong, I think, about what poverty is.

Being poor has never meant only lacking the calories and shelter needed to stay alive. It has meant being unable to do what one's neighbours take for granted: to send a child to school in clothes that will not draw mockery, to return a dinner invitation, to keep a telephone so that an employer can call. These requirements are set by the society one lives in, and they rise as that society grows richer. A family that could once manage without a refrigerator or a bank account cannot easily do so when shops, schools and employers assume that it has both. Relative lines track this moving threshold of participation, and that is exactly why their indifference to a uniform rise in incomes is not a defect. If everyone's income doubled, the cost of taking part in ordinary life would roughly double too.

This does not mean that relative measures can stand alone. Their weakness shows most plainly in a recession. When median income falls, the line falls with it, and a household whose income has not changed may be counted as having escaped poverty while its circumstances are no better, and its anxieties perhaps worse. A measure that reports falling poverty in the middle of a slump will strike most people as perverse, and they will be right. Absolute lines, fixed in real terms at some past standard, have the opposite virtue: they register whether the poorest are gaining or losing ground in purchasing power, whatever is happening to everyone else.

The sensible conclusion is not to choose between the two but to read them together, as answers to different questions. An absolute line asks whether the poor can buy more than they could before; a relative line asks whether they can still live as members of the society around them. A government that improves the first while the second worsens has achieved something real, but it has not abolished poverty, and it should not be allowed to claim that it has.
